claim: The CAS documentation consolidation uses a four-phase pipeline: freeze the corpus, map documents to durable claims, classify and verify claims against code at HEAD, and reduce the verified ledger into current documentation.
Consolidation artifacts live under `docs/superpowers/cas/consolidation-2026-08/` and are committed so every pipeline phase is restartable and auditable.
The consolidated user-facing CAS documentation is placed under `docs/en/antalya/cas/`, with the old corpus retained only when it is still valuable and still actual.
New pages under `docs/en/` require frontmatter fields `description`, `sidebar_label`, `sidebar_position`, `slug`, `title`, and `doc_type`, and every heading requires an explicit kebab-case anchor.
The supported platform wording for CAS object storage is: AWS and GCP work, Azure probably works, and other S3-compatible stores require atomic or conditional operations such as `If-None-Match`.
Published CAS pages are intended to be skimmable in about two minutes, use short prose with tables and Mermaid diagrams, and stay below a 300-line soft limit and a 500-line hard limit.
Files ending in `.tla` or `.cfg` are never modified or deleted by the CAS documentation consolidation.
Deletion of old CAS documentation occurs only in Task 16 and only after the user approves the coverage matrix.

`docs/superpowers/cas/BACKLOG.md` remains at its existing path as a permanent live file during consolidation, while `deferred-docs-fixes.md` remains an active append target until its concurrent writer stops.

The frozen CAS corpus includes changed markdown/text files relative to the merge-base with `altinity/antalya-26.6`, selected untracked CAS-related markdown/text files, and explicit `utils/ca-soak/scenarios/` documents, while excluding `.tla` and `.cfg` files.
Map records represent one self-contained durable claim rather than a document summary, and play-by-play run statuses, task checkboxes, night logs, and review sign-offs produce no records.
The map gate requires every corpus file to be accounted for, every JSONL record to be valid, every source path to exist, and every record ID to be unique.
Verification agents receive claim and cluster JSON but not the source documents; evidence must come from code at HEAD rather than from the statement that a document says the claim.
Verification verdicts distinguish `done`, `rejected`, `stale`, `open`, `doc-fact`, `unverifiable`, and `ephemeral`, and verdict evidence is pinned to the checked Git commit.
The verification phase mechanically treats `history` claims routed to `none` as `ephemeral` or `unverifiable` because they cannot be checked against implementation code.
A random five-percent adversarial audit rechecks `done` and `stale` verdicts because a false `done` can lose work and a false `stale` can lose knowledge.
CAS configuration examples must be executed against a live server before publication, including the SQL in `quick-start.md` and the `MOVE PARTITION` workflow in `migration.md`.
The public CAS roadmap is derived from verified `done`, user-visible `open`, known-limitations, and deliberately-rejected claims, while internal issue IDs are omitted from the public page.
The internal CAS backlog preserves existing issue IDs, moves `done` and `rejected` items to a terminal consolidation section, and keeps `open` items in the live section.
`docs/superpowers/cas/AGENTS.md` is a persistent survivor that consolidates branch invariants, test recipes, delegation policy, known traps, and pointers for future agents.
The coverage matrix maps every corpus file to a destination, an `ephemeral` reason, or `KEEP-IN-PLACE`, and deletion is forbidden if any file has no fate.
The target CAS architecture documentation uses `blob`, part manifest, ref, `RefLedger`, mount lease, `server_root_id`, and incarnation token as canonical vocabulary across pages.

`manifests-and-refs.md` and `garbage-collection.md` receive strict HEAD verification because the ref/GC subsystem changed after the walkthrough, including the v5 invariant reset, contiguous streams, `_ckpt`, catalog, and Stage A/B work.

The CAS corpus consolidation exists because roughly 390 markdown/text files contain both obsolete material and durable contracts, design decisions, bugs, TODOs, and runbook facts that plain deletion would lose.
The new CAS documentation set reworks the numbered internal documents `01`–`11` into the architecture section under `docs/en/antalya/cas/`.
Still-valuable, still-actual CAS specifications remain where they are as `KEEP-IN-PLACE`; other old corpus files are deleted only after coverage review.
`docs/superpowers/cas/BACKLOG.md` remains the internal working backlog, with issue IDs preserved and never renumbered, while `roadmap.md` is the public curated roadmap.
The CAS reliability story is based on TLA+/TLC model checking, corner-case testing, and multi-hour chaos-tested soak runs.
CAS is described as experimental because the code is actively cleaned up and backward-incompatible format changes remain possible, while the implementation is intended to work correctly today.
The ref/GC subsystem has the highest documentation drift because Stage B landed on 2026-08-03 after the walkthrough, so current code takes precedence over the walkthrough for those pages.
An extraction manifest gives every corpus file either `records: N` or an `ephemeral` reason; every durable record has one claim, source paths, issue IDs, and one suggested target.
A `done` verdict means implemented at HEAD and requires `file:symbol` or test evidence, while an `open` verdict means the claim is still actual and absent at HEAD.

A `rejected` verdict requires a conscious decision pointer and reason, a `stale` verdict requires what HEAD contradicts, and an `unverifiable` verdict requires an explanation of why code cannot check the claim.

Routing sends `done` and `rejected` material to `roadmap.md` and BACKLOG strike-throughs, `open` material to the regroomed `BACKLOG.md`, `doc-fact` material to its target page, and `stale` or `ephemeral` material only to the coverage matrix.
Verification is scoped to claims that enter new documentation, enter BACKLOG as `open`, or justify removal; `ephemeral` and `history` claims are not verified against code.
The Gate D coverage matrix is reviewed by the user before deletion, and `.tla`, `.cfg`, and `KEEP-IN-PLACE` files remain untouched.
The full historical narrative remains in Git history for a future blog post, while the public `architecture/design-history.md` is a condensed version of `how-we-got-here.md`.

The final consolidation state keeps the new documentation set, regroomed `BACKLOG.md`, `AGENTS.md`, selected still-actual specifications, all model sources and `*_RESULTS.md`, and only the coverage matrix from the work directory.
The metadata storage type string is changed from `content_addressed` to `cas`, and no compatibility alias is retained because the branch is unreleased.
The canonical CAS spelling is `CAS` in CamelCase identifiers, SQL keywords, grants, and prose, and `cas` in snake_case table names, settings, config keys, test names, and tags.

The SQL commands are renamed to `SYSTEM CAS GC RUN`, `SYSTEM CAS GC REBUILD`, `SYSTEM CAS GC START`, `SYSTEM CAS GC STOP`, `SYSTEM CAS FSCK`, `SYSTEM CAS DROP POOL MEMBER`, and `SYSTEM CAS FORGET`, with access types renamed from `CONTENT_ADDRESSED_*` to `CAS_*`.
The registered system table names are `cas_log`, `cas_gc_log`, and `cas_mounts`; the corresponding C++ class names remain unchanged.
The CAS server setting names are `cas_blob_upload_pool_size` and `cas_condemned_upload_memory_bytes`.
The dead legacy disk-config keys `content_addressed_allow_shared_pool` and `content_addressed_gc_grace_sec` are not read and are removed from the skip-list and every configuration that sets them.

The replication part-fetch HTTP names are `cas_pool_uuid`, `cas_relink`, `cas_confirm`, `cas_source_token`, and `cas_confirm_answer`, and mixed-build clusters must be fully rebuilt because version skew silently falls back to non-CAS full copies.

Identifiers belonging to compare-and-swap rather than the CAS feature are excluded from naming changes, including `casPut`, `CasOutcome`, `CasResult`, `CasOp::Cas`, `CasOp::CasConflict`, and the `CasRequestControl.h` family.

Internal C++ names such as namespace `DB::Cas`, classes `CasPool`, `CasGc`, `CasLayout`, and `CasMountRuntime`, and files such as `ContentAddressedLog.cpp` remain unchanged by user-facing naming unification.
Per-disk CAS settings such as `scratch_path`, `gc_enabled`, and `server_root_id` remain unprefixed because they are scoped by their disk block.
The naming effort does not add compatibility aliases for old SQL, metadata type, or wire-protocol names because the branch is unreleased.
The CAS gtest suite prefix is `CAS*`, while `CascadeWriteBuffer` remains excluded because its `Cas` substring is unrelated to CAS.
The CAS test tag is `no-cas-storage`, and the runner flags are `--cas-storage` and `--cas-s3-storage`.
The accepted metadata storage type spelling is `cas`, and `system.disks.metadata_type` renders it as `CAS`.
The CAS system log configuration sections are `<cas_log>` and `<cas_gc_log>`, corresponding to the tables `system.cas_log` and `system.cas_gc_log`.
The naming plan changes the five part-fetch protocol literals in `DataPartsExchange.cpp` atomically within one build and updates integration-test assertions to match them.
The obscure-name cleanup changes CamelCase `Gc` to `GC`, `Ckpt` to `Checkpoint`, `Txns` to `Transactions`, and `Dedup` to `Deduplication` in user-facing CAS names.
The user-facing `system.cas_mounts` columns are `started_at` and `expires_at`, both retaining type `DateTime64(3)`.
The user-facing `system.cas_log` names are column `generation`, event type `indegree_zero`, detail key `prev_indegree`, and object kind `snapshot`.
The user-facing `system.cas_gc_log` columns include `server_root_id` and `phase_duration_microseconds`.
The per-disk CAS settings are `deduplication_cache_bytes`, `deduplication_head_first_min_bytes`, and `gc_snapshot_generations_to_keep`.

The derived asynchronous metric `ReaderExecutorModeledCostMsPerRequestedMiB` is removed, while ProfileEvents `ReaderExecutorModeledCostMicroseconds` and `ReaderExecutorRequestedBytes` remain available for observers to compute the ratio.
The `clickhouse-disks` CAS commands are `cas-fsck`, `cas-gc-dryrun`, `cas-gc-rebuild`, `cas-inspect`, and `cas-drop-member`; the deprecated bare `fsck` alias is removed.
Persisted CAS object-storage format strings, including the serialization key `gen` and `_snap` and `_ckpt` object-name suffixes, are not renamed by the obscure-name cleanup.
On RustFS, a ref-log enumeration returned sequence `0x1430e` while omitting predecessors `0x1430c` and `0x1430d` during a soak.
The omitted ref-log objects were durable for about 19 seconds before the anomaly, and an exact-key `HEAD` at the disagreement time confirmed that both were present.
Across 65,263 ref-log uploads in the affected namespace, partitioned by epoch, zero uploads were out of order.
Concurrent delete, stale-epoch minting, out-of-order appends, and a late `Unresolved` PUT were excluded as explanations for the RustFS omission by evidence at three source levels.
The LIST anomaly had a correct tail; the lie was omission of predecessors below the returned frontier rather than tail under-reporting.

Predecessor omission below a correct LIST tail is legal on contract-compliant S3 for writes concurrent with a paginated enumeration because S3 provides no snapshot contract for keys landing during the walk.
The observed RustFS omission was a contract violation because the omitted keys were durable about 19 seconds before the enumeration began.
Tail under-reporting of a completed write is illegal on a compliant store under the read-after-write clause and is the only LIST property a per-backend trust mode may rely on.
No LIST violation has been observed on AWS S3; the incident is evidence about RustFS and legal enumeration concurrency, not AWS behavior.

During the incident, exact-key `GET` and `HEAD` remained truthful while LIST was not, and conditional writes were trusted because `putIfAbsent` cannot report `Created` over an existing key without data loss.
The CAS GC trust chain is catalog cut, `_ckpt` acknowledged frontier, exact `GET` records, and conditional-write fences; LIST is only a hint for work bounds, witness sets, and genesis.
Stale-but-honest reads create a true historical cut whose errors cause retention or delay, while a fabricated cut from omission under a seal can authorize unrecoverable destruction.
Three hammer runs listing about 19 million keys produced zero holes before the rare LIST violation occurred live within four minutes of an ordinary soak.
A mount-time one-shot synthetic LIST probe cannot certify a backend because it can pass on RustFS even though a rare load- and timing-dependent violation later occurs.
A CAS bucket passport can be operator attestation per bucket, continuous verification with auto-revocation, or both; trust is a runtime property of a bucket rather than a backend type string.
The fail-close default for LIST trust is probe-always, and RustFS currently fails the proposed passport by measurement.

CAS GC optimization must retain arithmetic middle intake everywhere, frontier probes for held or logless namespaces, and `tail < cursor` quality detection; only `tail == cursor` can prove a trusted frontier under a bucket passport.

`copyObjectConditional` can fall back to an unconditional read/write copy after `AccessDenied` or unsupported multipart-copy paths, allowing a concurrent CAS promotion to be overwritten; conditional operations must fail closed.
Resurrection of a condemned object can overwrite a live incarnation installed by another writer because the rewrite is not bound to the observed token with `If-Match`.
`CasObjectStorageBackend::get` and `getStream` can return bytes from one object version with the size and identity token obtained by an earlier `HEAD` from another version.
A failed Condemned-marker write can let GC delete a newly referenced blob because condemnation failures are swallowed and writers treat absent or Clean metadata as live.

Pre-CAS retention can delete data referenced by the currently adopted GC snapshot because pruning protects only the proposed seal's generations rather than the union of parent and proposed references.
Relink replication can delete blobs during the sender-to-receiver gap because the sender releases its source edge before receiver precommit and no durable handoff or pin spans receiver commit.
Relink can advertise pool A while reservation selects a local disk or pool B, allowing pool B to publish references to bodies that exist only in A.

Manual GC, rebuild, and system-table access can race metadata shutdown because scheduler pointers and `cas_store` are used after mutex unlock and lazy creation can resurrect the scheduler after shutdown.
Decommissioning can delete a successor mount's control objects because it releases the administrative claim before rereading and deleting current epoch, owner, and mount objects.
The CAS event sink has an unsynchronized assignment/read race because renewal threads can read a shared `std::function` while `setEventSink` assigns it.
Namespace removal can miss a build between allocation and registration, allowing a paused build to publish `NamespaceBirth` after cancellation and resurrect the removed namespace.

`removeDirectory`, `removeRecursive`, and committed `moveDirectory` mutate durable refs immediately rather than through a rollback-capable transaction overlay, so aborting can leave durable refs changed and can publish a supposedly removed part.

A propagating telemetry exception after durable ref publication can leave transaction state inconsistent: the caller sees failure while a live ref exists and the transaction lacks the ref for success or rollback.

Default CAS deduplication relies on collision-prone `CityHash128` without rehashing or comparing stored bytes, so an untrusted shared-pool writer can substitute attacker-controlled bytes after a chosen collision.
Local or NFS multi-server pools can start with per-process conditional-operation emulation that violates CAS and GC invariants, because the implementation logs an INFO message and continues.
With `use_reader_executor=1`, CAS reads can expose the envelope header and use incorrect offsets because `ReadPipeline` rejects unsupported cache/decryption stages but not `file_view`.
Unknown GCS bucket-versioning state fails open: inability to determine versioning only logs and continues, although enabled versioning archives generations and prevents GC from reclaiming storage.
The emulated Local backend returns monotonic emulation tokens for exact operations but ETag/mtime tokens from LIST, so GC exact deletes based on listing tokens fail.
Native conditional mutations ignore `Token.type` and send only `Token.value`, allowing a same-text token from a different token dialect to authorize a mutation.
Safety-critical CAS decoders accept incomplete or duplicate records and unbound fold generations, so a misplaced seal can authorize skipped references.
Compatibility versions are narrowed before validation, so a value such as `4294967299` can truncate to `3` and pass current-version validation.
`gc_interval_sec=0` can spin the scheduler and `gc_shards=0` can persist unreadable `gcs=0` state because bounds are not validated before opening the pool.
`truncateFile` reports success without changing bytes, so callers can observe successful truncation while old content remains.
`removeFile` discards the `if_exists` flags and succeeds when a file is missing even for the non-`ifExists` API instead of throwing `FILE_DOESNT_EXIST`.
Retrying a failed commit can report success with refs absent because rollback removes published refs but leaves staging entries marked `published`, causing retry to skip them.
Concurrent verbatim append can lose updates because CAS retry reuses stale `old + suffix` data instead of rereading the winner's value; the path is used for mutation-entry CSN append.
Rename treats an unrelated existing destination as successful replay when the source is absent, even though no operation ID or content proof exists.

Part-write construction failure can permanently pin the active-build watermark because the active sequence is inserted before `PartWriteTxn` construction and no destructor retires it after allocation or event-sink failure.
The new metadata storage can be selected directly with `metadata_type=content_addressed` without an `allow_experimental_*` gate.
`system.content_addressed_mounts` can silently return partial results when obtaining the pool or listing mounts fails because the exception is caught and omitted.
Explicit `staging_backend=s3` can silently fall back to local staging after conditional-copy capability probing fails, hiding configuration errors and unexpectedly consuming local disk.
A scenario card must only populate `result` and drive the cluster through framework helpers; it must not call `result.finalize()`, write reports, or modify `RUN_HISTORY` or `BACKLOG`.
A registered scenario requires `name`, `title`, and `priority`; optional flags include `abandons`, `expect_exception`, `compose_variant`, `needs_infra`, and `param_table`.
A scenario with `needs_infra` set is marked inconclusive and its `run` method is not executed when the two-replica plus RustFS compose cannot provide the required infrastructure.

`RunContext` exposes cluster nodes with `query`, `command`, `scalar`, `container`, and `ping`, and provides `params`, `seed`, `duration_s`, `scale`, logging, artifact paths, subdirectories, and JSON/text writers.
`Verdict.inconclusive` represents unavailable data and must not be silently converted to pass; `Verdict.skipped` explicitly records that an assertion was not evaluated.
`standard_end` quiesces the cluster, settles fsck, drives forced GC to a fixpoint, runs final fsck and dry-run checks, collects observations, dumps raw extracts, and runs common hard assertions.
`insert_values` should use deterministic `SELECT ... FROM numbers(N)` content for deduplication tests because `randomString` is non-deterministic.

`cluster_events_snapshot` and `cluster_events_delta` observe `Cas*`, `DiskS3*`, and `S3*` events, while `ca_event_counts_all` classifies bad events including `read_missing`, `dangling_access`, `corrupt_dangle`, `corrupt_decode`, `snap_journal_incoherent`, and `exception`.
GC driving uses one leader via `gc.gc_round` or `gc.gc_drive_round`; callers must not drive both leaders concurrently because that can cause a concurrent-leader reclaim leak.
Scenario cards must never silently skip an assertion and must emit `Verdict.inconclusive` or `Verdict.skipped` with a reason when evaluation is unavailable.
Negative soak cards set `expect_exception=True`, assert the expected error code, prove no live ref points to missing content with `fsck dangling==0`, and verify partial uploads are reclaimable.
Scenario table names use the scenario ID as a prefix, such as `s09_wide`, so cards do not collide and `table_filter` can scope quiescence.
The soak compose infrastructure has two ClickHouse replicas `ch1` and `ch2`, RustFS, and a single-node Keeper, with a `gc_shards2` variant using `gc_shards=2`.
Soak runs bind-mount the host-built binary from `../../build/programs/clickhouse`, and record `version()` plus the repository Git SHA in `config.json`.
The CAS capability probe requires an object store that enforces conditional operations, including wrong-token DELETE returning 412; the suite therefore uses RustFS `1.0.0-beta.8`, not MinIO.
A fresh soak pool is created by `docker compose down -v` followed by `up -d`, because the compose RustFS container is ephemeral and teardown wipes the fixed `test/soak_pool/` prefix.
`--no-reset` reuses the current pool, and its first run is not a clean-pool run.
The default soak scale is `dev`, while `--scale ci` is medium and `--scale full` targets specification-scale workloads such as S01 100 GiB, S03 1–10M objects, and S05 10000 tables.
A passing dev-scale soak is never treated as specification-scale validation because each card records its actual scale and verdict.

S12 requires ten replicas, S22 requires a fault-injecting S3 proxy, S24 requires a tiny `deduplication_cache_bytes`, S27 requires unstable or duplicate LIST pages, S15 requires `gc_shards=8`, and S23 requires one-server and ten-server idle variants; the two-replica compose cannot exercise these cases, while S20 covers the two-replica fetch/relink proxy.
S18 may encounter the pre-existing `B3` freeze/shadow bug; the card records a freeze failure as inconclusive with a backlog anomaly instead of a hard failure.

S07 treats manifest caps of 1M entries, 256 MiB encoded, 16 MiB inline, and 1 MiB largest inline as fail-closed properties, recording inconclusive when dev-scale SQL cannot deterministically reach a cap.

The primary soak correctness oracle is all-replica agreement on `count() + sum(sipHash64(*))`, with an absolute Python-side prediction for deterministic `INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM numbers(N)` workloads.
Structural soak correctness uses `clickhouse-disks cas-fsck` with `dangling==0` and the `cas-gc-dryrun ⊆ unreachable` oracle only at quiesced checkpoints.
`SYSTEM CAS GC RUN ca` performs one synchronous GC round on the contacted node, and only the lease holder makes progress.
A forced GC fixpoint drive issues rounds on both replicas until fsck unreachable count settles; for a non-abandoning scenario the expected final `unreachable` count is zero.
S25 probes the deprecated or likely blocked `Ordinary` engine and records the exact behavior as inconclusive if the engine is blocked.
S10 probes lightweight delete and patch-part support at runtime; unsupported subpaths are inconclusive, while lightweight `DELETE` correctness is still tested.
